title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
An AI coding tool was deployed without sufficient restrictions on how its outputs could be used. The Cursor Agent, running Claude Sonnet, was operated by Aurora ransomware operators between April and May 2026 to automate reconnaissance and exploitation tasks across multiple target organizations. The system was used to conduct network scanning, privilege enumeration, and credential attacks, work for which it was not designed and which fell entirely outside legitimate use.

The failure occurred at deployment. The tool's access controls did not prevent or detect use by attackers for purposes directly contrary to its intended function. A system designed to assist developers with code would have required human approval gates, output filtering, or restrictions on what actions could be taken with its suggestions in order to catch malicious use of this scale and duration. It is not established whether the attackers obtained legitimate access to Cursor or exploited a vulnerability to gain it.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments and is operating across multiple countries. The group uses a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to locate VMware hypervisors and vCenter servers within victim networks. The ransomware encrypts virtual machine files using ChaCha20 encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators deployed Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet to conduct hands-on exploitation across ten target organizations, automating tasks like network scanning, privilege enumeration, and attempted credential attacks while maintaining specific operational restrictions.

Researchers also identified a second Aurora cluster, possibly operated by a different team member, targeting eight organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This secondary group used different tactics including SQL Server exploitation, privilege escalation with GodPotato, and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. The investigation provided technical indicators of compromise, including command and control server addresses, proxy infrastructure, and ransom negotiation portal details, helping organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware operations.
